readerTitle: Why the same brunch has a line on Sunday and empty tables on Tuesday
caseNote: 가상 사례 (브런치 카페, 소프트웨어 온보딩) + 실제 관찰 (미국 조류독감과 달걀 가격)
insight: 가격, 줄, 재고가 변하면 먼저 수요 쪽이 움직였는지 공급 쪽이 움직였는지 묻는다. 원인에 따라 맞는 대응이 달라진다.
misconception: 가격은 판매자가 원가에 마진을 붙여 정하는 것이고, 가격이 오르면 판매자가 욕심을 부린 것이다.

sources.text: 경제학 표준 개념 (수요, 공급, 균형 가격, 부족과 과잉)
USDA Economic Research Service, egg markets and highly pathogenic avian influenza (2022–2023, 2025)
카페와 소프트웨어 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 미국에서 2022년과 2025년 조류독감으로 산란계가 대량 살처분되어 달걀 가격이 크게 올랐다는 내용은 USDA ERS 자료로 게시 전 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 구체적 수치(살처분 수, 가격 상승률)를 넣지 않고 "millions of hens"로만 적었습니다.
카페와 소프트웨어 사례의 대기 시간(45분, 5주) 등 수치는 모두 설명용 가상 수치입니다.

cards.title: Why the same brunch has a line on Sunday and empty tables on Tuesday
body: Same café. Same menu. Same prices. On Sunday at 11, people wait 45 minutes for eggs. On Tuesday at 11, half the tables are empty.
The food didn't change. Something else did, and it decides more of your prices than your costs do.

image.label: One café shown twice: crowded Sunday, quiet Tuesday
image.brief: 화면을 좌우로 나눈 같은 카페. 왼쪽 "Sunday"는 문밖까지 긴 줄과 꽉 찬 테이블, 오른쪽 "Tuesday"는 빈 테이블과 한가한 직원. 메뉴판과 가격은 양쪽이 똑같음. 실제 상호나 로고 없음.

cards.title: Your brunch café is two different businesses.
body: You have 40 seats. On Sundays the wait hits 45 minutes and some people give up and leave. On Tuesdays you barely cover staff.
Your partner says it's time to change something. What do you do?

options.text: Raise every price 15%, since the Sunday line proves people will pay
options.feedback: Sunday might absorb it, but Tuesday was already too quiet. A higher price there pushes away the few customers you have.

options.text: Treat the days separately: a pricier Sunday set menu, and a reason to come on weekdays
options.feedback: You charge more where people want more than you can seat, and work to draw people where you have seats to spare. It takes more planning and clear communication.

options.text: Keep prices and hire two more Sunday staff to turn tables faster
options.feedback: Faster tables add capacity, which helps. But it adds wages, the 40 seats still cap you, and Tuesday stays empty.

cards.title: On Sunday, customers pay in time.
body: On Sunday, more people want a table than you have tables. The menu price stays fixed, so the extra demand shows up somewhere else: **the line**. Customers pay with 45 minutes of waiting.
On Tuesday, the seats are the same but far fewer people want them. Nothing is wrong with the food. There just aren't enough buyers at that price, on that day.

cards.title: Supply and demand
body: **Demand** is how much people want to buy at each price. Higher price, fewer buyers. **Supply** is how much sellers will offer at each price. Higher price, more sellers willing to offer it.
Where the two meet, buyers and sellers agree. Set the price below that point and you get a shortage: lines and sold-out signs. Set it above and you get a surplus: empty tables and leftover stock.

image.label: Demand and supply lines crossing, with shortage and surplus zones
image.brief: 단순한 그래프. 아래로 내려가는 "Demand" 선과 위로 올라가는 "Supply" 선이 교차, 교차점에 "Market price". 교차점 아래 가격에는 "Shortage: lines" (작은 줄 선 사람 아이콘), 위 가격에는 "Surplus: empty tables" (빈 의자 아이콘). 축 숫자 없음.

cards.title: Either side can move the price.
body: Prices change when one side shifts. Demand moves with weather, holidays, paydays and trends. Supply moves with harvests, wages, new competitors and broken equipment.

Eggs are a clear case. When bird flu forced US farms to cull millions of hens in 2022 and again in 2025, egg prices jumped. People weren't suddenly eating more eggs. **Supply fell**, and the same demand met fewer eggs.
cards.callout: Same symptom, higher price. Different cause, different fix.
cards.softwareNote: Extra copies of software cost almost nothing, so the squeeze shows up in what's limited: engineer time, support hours, server capacity, ad slots. That's where supply and demand bite.

cards.title: You are also a buyer.
body: Supply and demand set what you pay, too. If five new restaurants open on your street, they all compete for the same cooks. More demand for the same number of cooks means higher wages.
That isn't a cost problem you can fix by negotiating harder. It's the market for cooks moving. The useful question is which side moved, and whether it will stay that way.

cards.title: The picture is simple. Reading it isn't.
body: You never see the demand line directly. You only see clues: lines, sell-outs, unsold stock. And a spike can be temporary, like one viral post or one holiday week.

Raising prices into a shortage also has a cost beyond the math. Customers judge whether a price feels fair, and a sudden jump can cost goodwill that took years to build. Sometimes a line is worth keeping.

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: Your plan includes a free live setup call with your team. After a viral post, sign-ups doubled. The wait for a setup call is now five weeks, and some new users cancel before they ever get one.

options.text: Cut the plan's price to grow even faster while attention is high
options.feedback: That adds more demand to the part that's already short. The wait gets longer and more users cancel before setup.

options.text: Make live setup a paid add-on and build a self-serve setup guide
options.feedback: The fee cools demand for scarce team time, and the guide adds supply that never runs out. Some users will dislike paying for what used to be free.

options.text: Hire three more onboarding staff right away
options.feedback: More supply does shrink the wait, but hiring takes months and adds fixed cost. If the spike fades, you're overstaffed.

cards.title: When something changes, ask which side moved.
body: Lines, sell-outs, empty seats and price jumps are signals from supply and demand. Find out whether buyers or sellers shifted before you decide what to do.
**Try it today:** pick one thing in your business that's always short or always left over. Write down whether the cause is on the demand side or the supply side.
